title: Anisotropic mesoscale magnetic scattering across the spin-reorientation transition in TbMn6Sn6
authors: Zhuang Xu, Fan Chen, Hui Cheng, Xinmin Wang, Taisen Zuo, He Cheng, Haitao Hu, Cuiping Zhang, Qian Zhao, Michel Kenzelmann, Jonathan S. White, Junying Shen, Xin Tong
abstract: TbMn6Sn6 is a centrosymmetric ferrimagnetic kagome metal that combines topological electronic states with strong magnetic anisotropy and a near-room-temperature spin-reorientation transition (SRT). Real-space imaging studies of thin specimens have revealed helical stripes, biskyrmion-like textures, and skyrmion-bubble-like structures in the spin-reorientation regime. Whether such local textures develop into a bulk long-range-ordered skyrmion lattice remains unresolved. Here we present small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) results probing the mesoscale magnetism of a bulk TbMn6Sn6 single crystal. We observe no sixfold SANS Bragg pattern indicative of a long-range-ordered skyrmion lattice under the explored conditions. Instead, the dominant magnetic response is an anisotropic twofold low-Q scattering component whose intensity distribution and field dependence evolve markedly across the spin-reorientation regime. In zero field, a broad and horizontally elongated low-Q signal develops above TSR and weakens as the system approaches the paramagnetic state. At 345 K with H || b, the signal is diffuse and is suppressed rapidly below about 700 Oe. By contrast, at 310 K with H || c, close to TSR, the response is more concentrated and line-shaped and persists to higher fields. The contrasts between these scans likely reflect the combined effects of rapidly evolving magnetic anisotropy near TSR and the field geometry. Our results therefore establish a bulk anisotropic mesoscale magnetic response across the spin-reorientation regime, consistent with stripe- or domain-related textures reported by real-space imaging, while not uniquely identifying their real-space morphology.
summary: This experimental study uses small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) to investigate the magnetic structure of TbMn6Sn6 across its spin-reorientation transition. The research rules out the formation of a bulk, long-range skyrmion lattice, instead characterizing a highly anisotropic mesoscale magnetic response. This work confirms that the magnetic correlations are dominated by stripe or domain-like textures whose characteristics strongly depend on the applied magnetic field and temperature.
main_problem: The study aims to determine if local magnetic textures observed in thin specimens of TbMn6Sn6 develop into a bulk long-range-ordered skyrmion lattice across the spin-reorientation transition (SRT).
main_result: The authors found no sixfold SANS Bragg pattern indicative of a long-range skyrmion lattice; instead, the dominant response is an anisotropic twofold low-Q scattering component evolving markedly across the SRT.
method: Small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) was used on a bulk single crystal, probing mesoscale magnetism by measuring the evolution of the low-Q scattering component under varying magnetic fields and temperatures.
model_or_system: The physical system is TbMn6Sn6, a centrosymmetric ferrimagnetic kagome metal exhibiting strong magnetic anisotropy and a near-room-temperature spin-reorientation transition. The analysis compares bulk scattering data to real-space imaging results.
key_observables: Anisotropic twofold low-Q scattering component, SANS Bragg patterns (specifically the absence of sixfold peaks), and the field/temperature dependence of the scattering intensity and the inverse-q descriptor (d).
important_parameters: Spin-reorientation temperature (TSR $\sim 310$ K), applied magnetic fields ($H \parallel b$ and $H \parallel c$), and mesoscale length scales probed by SANS.
main_assumptions: The observed scattering is attributed to stripe- or domain-related textures, and the analysis relies on interpreting the field-dependent contrast evolution rather than assuming a unique real-space periodicity.
figures_summary: Figures show the evolution of the low-Q signal across the SRT, comparing field dependence at different temperatures (e.g., $H \parallel b$ at $345$ K vs. $H \parallel c$ at $310$ K), and include robustness checks using high-field-reference subtraction.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the context by noting the discrepancy between real-space imaging and bulk measurements. It then presents SANS results showing the anisotropic, field-dependent low-Q scattering across the SRT, concluding that the response is mesoscale and anisotropic, consistent with domain structures but not a long-range skyrmion lattice.
why_interesting: While the focus is on magnetism, the study of phase transitions (SRT) and the evolution of correlated states (mesoscale textures) under external fields provides insights into many-body dynamics and symmetry breaking, which are relevant to understanding complex quantum many-body systems.

(b) Single-crystal X-ray diffraction pattern. (c) Temperature-dependent magnetization for B ∥ab, identifying the spin-reorientation transition. (d) Field-dependent magnetization for H ∥b at representative temperatures.

Figure 2: Zero-field temperature scan in the beam ∥b geometry. (a) Background-subtracted SANS patterns. (b,c) Temperature dependences of I and d. A broad horizontal twofold low-Q signal appears above approximately 310 K and persists below about 400 K.

Figure 3: Field scan at 345 K in the beam ∥b, field ∥b geometry. (a) Background-subtracted SANS patterns. (b,c) Field dependences of I and d. I and d decrease up to about 700 Oe and become nearly field independent from 700 to 2000 Oe.

Figure 3 shows the field scan at 345 K for beam ∥b and H ∥b. The low-Q response is broad and diffuse. Its integrated intensity falls rapidly up to about 700 Oe and changes only weakly at higher fields; d decreases over the same low-field interval and then approaches a plateau. At 345 K, above TSR and within the high-temperature easy-plane regime, the magnetic anisotropy has evolved toward the high-temperature easy-plane state [22, 23, 24]. An in-plane field can therefore align the magnetization comparatively efficiently, providing a natural explanation for the rapid loss of the anisotropic low-Q contrast.
